title: Connecting the Dots, A Series on MTSS at My School
author: Elana
summary: This installment closes out a multi-part series on implementing Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), arguing that the standard failure mode in school reform is treating professional learning as a one-and-done workshop rather than an ongoing process paired with job-embedded coaching. The piece specifies four non-negotiable areas schools must invest sustained time in if MTSS is to function as a genuine reform framework rather than paperwork: developing a strong Tier 1 curriculum first, building staff data literacy, establishing clear intervention protocols, and practicing structured data-based decision making. It offers a concrete sequence for schools starting this work, beginning with a needs-assessment tool to locate which MTSS components already exist and which are missing, followed by fidelity checks on the core Tier 1 curriculum that explicitly acknowledge no curriculum works exactly as written in every classroom. The piece pushes specifically on data literacy as a practiced skill rather than a training-day checkbox, asking whether school leaders have actually modeled real data conversations at the school, grade, group, and individual student level rather than assuming staff can interpret data reports unaided. It closes with a warning against MTSS becoming another layer of forms and discussion without action, insisting the entire framework only functions if teams return to concrete steps repeatedly to analyze, discuss, and adjust, the actual mechanism of continuous improvement.
points: Names the standard failure mode in school reform explicitly: one-and-done professional learning workshops do not move the needle, because staff need both the why and the how, supported by ongoing job-embedded coaching, not a single training day.

Specifies four non-negotiable investment areas for genuine MTSS implementation: developing Tier 1 curriculum first, building staff data literacy, establishing intervention protocols, and practicing structured data-based decision making, arguing all four require sustained time, not a single rollout.

Frames Tier 1 curriculum fidelity checks as a balance rather than rigid compliance, explicitly asking whether staff can remain faithful to evidence-based practices while still adapting a curriculum that 'does not fit every setting all the time exactly as it was written.'

Treats data literacy as a practiced skill requiring modeled data conversations at the school, grade-level, group, and individual student level, rather than assuming staff can interpret screening and progress-monitoring data without structured practice.

Warns explicitly against MTSS collapsing into paperwork, insisting the framework only functions as continuous improvement if teams treat each step as something to return to, analyze, discuss, and adjust rather than a form to file away.
quotes: One thing we know about professional learning, both from research and experience, is that one and done workshops or learning sessions do not move the needle in helping teachers apply their knowledge to the classroom. Educators must understand the why but also the how before we can apply our learning.

If school systems are serious about using Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) as a framework or umbrella for school reform, then schools need to spend time on the following areas: Developing Tier 1 First, Data Literacy Training, Intervention Protocols, Data-Based Decision Making.

Remember, no curriculum fits every setting all the time exactly as it was written. Can you be faithful to evidence-based and research-based practices while still having fidelity towards the curriculum?

Becoming data literate takes practice. Have you modeled data conversations while looking at school, grade-level, group, and student data? Do you have someone who could guide teacher teams through these discussions?

These steps mustn't be just part of a discussion, look good on paper, or produced into too many forms that schools are so good at developing. They must live in actionable steps that teams can come back to, analyze, discuss, and adjust. This is the very essence of the continuous improvement process.
